Man found dead on Flinders Island linked to shooting of police officer, Tasmanian authorities say

Body of a man in his 20s discovered by police who were sent to investigate the shooting of an officer, who is in a serious but stable condition

• Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

An on-duty police officer has been shot and a man found dead nearby as police investigate two firearm incidents in a tiny Tasmanian town.

The officer was working at Whitemark police station on Flinders Island, north-east of the island of Tasmania, when he was shot at about 9.45pm on Saturday night.

Police sent to investigate the shooting of the officer discovered the body of a man, believed to be in his mid-20s, with a gunshot wound on Walker Street, near the police station.

“At this time, police believe these two incidents are linked and that the situation has been safely contained,” Tasmanian police said in a statement on Sunday.

“Our thoughts are with the families and loved ones of those involved, and with the wider community of Flinders Island.”

The policeman is receiving treatment at the Royal Hobart hospital and remains in a serious but stable condition.

Whitemark has a population of about 300 according to the 2021 census, and the entire population of Flinders Island is fewer than 1,000 people.

Extra police resources, including forensic and uniformed officers, have been deployed to the island. Those with information about these incidents, including CCTV or dashcam footage of Walker Street, have been urged to contact police.

It is the second shooting of an on-duty police officer in Tasmania in 18 months. A Tasmanian officer was killed in the state’s north-west in June 2025 while executing a court-issued warrant to repossess a residence. The occupant of the home pleaded guilty to murder.

items.title: Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock
items.summary: Countries from nearly 200 countries are in a deadlock to try and get a new global climate agreement.
items.body:
Image source, Yasin Akgul/AFP/Getty Images

Image caption,

Panama's Environment Minister is pushing for language on fossil fuels to be in the final agreement

ByEsme Stallard

Senior climate and science journalist, Reporting fromAntalya, Turkey

Updated 3 hours ago

Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock, having run more than 24 hours into overtime as countries remain unable to agree on a new global climate deal.

In a late intervention on Friday, a group of countries led by France and Panama pushed back against the draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.

This still remains the main sticking point, along with a push from the Africa Group to get commitments on more money for adaptation - but the EU has previously said it would not support this.

Negotiating teams due to fly out on Sunday morning are now moving their flights to Monday in a sign that a deal is not in sight.

Not all countries have the funding or capacity to do this, and at some point the meeting could lose the critical number of nations needed to pass any global agreement.

This means the summit would end with no deal and have to be suspended. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.

• More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledgedPublished1 day ago

Ministers from island states, Panama, and a strong contingent of EU nations which include Spain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Finland have said they are pushing to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.

"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.

His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut.

She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.

"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.

For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - could acknowledge that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.

The world is entering a period called "overshoot".

Beyond this point scientists warn, external that millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.

The BBC understands that a number of other EU nations were asked to join the rebellion but declined, considering it unhelpful to negotiations.

Although one lead negotiator said he sympathised: "How can you have a climate agreement with no mention of the cause."

But Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister who is leading negotiations, pushed back.

He argued that this summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.

Away from COP, renewable energy is growing at unprecedented rates. For the first time this year a modern renewable source - solar panels - contributed the largest share of global energy demand growth, outstripping oil and gas, external.

The International Energy Agency also warned this week that the longer disruption to fuel supplies through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran War, the stronger the incentive to switch to electricity powered by renewables.

Although, this week US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed at a meeting in Shenzhen to increase oil production in the face of fuel supply disruption.

The 'worst' COP ever?

It is understood that one proposal is to keep fossil fuels off the table in exchange for Saudi Arabia and other petro-states signing up to a pledge for 35% of their energy consumption to come from electricity by 2035.

This does not solve one of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money.

Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (£91bn) by 2035 - that figure has now been removed.

"We did not come here to beg, we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.

Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.

"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.

These groups are normally highly critical of the process for not moving fast enough. But it seems that Turkey have been particularly unpopular as hosts after their lead negotiator walked out of some crucial negotiations leaving many countries feeling "disrespected", said one observer.

items.title: Lock of former US President George Washington's hair sells for $4,000
items.summary: The hair was given as a sign of friendship shortly before Washington's death in 1799, according to a descendent of its former owner.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

George Washington died in 1799 after serving for two terms as America's first president

A framed lock of hair from America's first president, George Washington, has been sold at auction for $4,000 (£3,058).

The hair once belonged to John Gadsby, who entertained Washington in 1799 just before the latter's death the same year, and was later obtained by a collector called John K Lattimer from a descendent of Gadsby's, according to Richmond Auctions, which sold the item.

Its new owner has not been named.

Saturday's sale is not the most expensive for Washington hair at auction. Three strands thought to have been removed from him close to or after his death stored in a locket sold for nearly $40,000 in 2021.

Gadsby, a resident of what in 1799 was the town of Alexandria in Virginia, entertained Washington for dinner shortly before his death later that year, according to a testament given in 1928 by Gadsby's granddaughter, Julia Ten Eyck McBlair, and which was posted on the Richmond Auctions website.

McBlair stated that her grandfather came into possession of Washington's hair "in view of the friendship and association with his last days" and had it framed and hung "under General Washington's portrait in our home in Washington City, there I have seen it all my life".

Gadsby hosted Washington's two birthday celebrations in 1798 and 1799, Richmond Auctions states.

Washington led American forces to victory against the British in the War of Independence and helped draft the US Constitution before becoming the country's first president in 1788. He stepped down in 1797 after serving two terms.

Several locks of Washington's hair have been preserved, including at least 50 examples that are in a collection at his former residence, Mount Vernon, which is now a museum.

"Public displays of hair from friends or loved ones peaked in the 19th century, but had long been popular among affluent families like the Washingtons," a blog on the Mount Vernon website states.

As well as lockets of his hair, other items associated with Washington have also done well at auction.

In July, a signed letter by Washington from 1776, in which he asks for soldiers for the Continental Army to fight the British, sold for $109,800.

items.title: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
items.summary: Fausto Isidro "Chapo Idisro" Meza Flores, who is accused of drug trafficking and torture, is detained after gun fight with authorities.
items.body:
Image source, FBI

Image caption,

Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained by Mexican special forces on Friday

ByTara Mewawalla

A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.

Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained along with his lieutenant by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.

Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.

Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.

Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores and his second-in-command, it added.

Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

A number of vehicles were pictured burning on a highway near Los Mochis, Sinaloa, after Fausto Isidro "Chapo Idisro" Meza Flores was arrested

The two detainees were subsequently flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said.

When he was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.

Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.

He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.

The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.

Meza Flores was originally a high-ranking member of the Beltrán Leyva Organization, but a split between rival factions led to a surge of violence and prompted him to establish his own cartel by 2013.

His organisation has also engaged in what US officials described as an "extremely violent turf war" with the Sinaloa Cartel, one of the most powerful drug trafficking gangs, which operates in the same region.

Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list after Mexican authorities reportedly linked his cartel to 20 million fentanyl pills they seized in 2024.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has taken a tougher stance on the country's cartels in a bid to resist US intervention on Mexican soil. Mexico has welcomed closer collaboration but resisted US boots on the ground.

Trump made stemming the flow of drugs into the US across its southern border one of his key election pledges.

items.title: Two groups verify mathematician’s claim that Claude helped prove mathematics problem
items.summary: Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge says it took six weeks for him using the AI tool to solve 19th-century Riemann hypothesis A mathematician at Anthropic has said that the San Francisco -based artificial intelligence (AI) company’s software has helped crack one of the most important unsolved problems in math…
items.body:
Alpöge said he solved the math problem using the Anthropic AI tool Claude a day after the company went public on the Nasdaq stock market index. Photograph: Brendan McDermid/Reuters

Alpöge said he solved the math problem using the Anthropic AI tool Claude a day after the company went public on the Nasdaq stock market index. Photograph: Brendan McDermid/Reuters

Anthropic mathematician claims he used Claude to prove 19th-century Riemann hypothesis

Levent Alpöge says it took six weeks for him using the AI tool to solve the math problem involving prime numbers

A mathematician at Anthropic is contending that the San Francisco-based artificial intelligence (AI) company’s software has helped crack one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.

Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician, on Friday posted a note on his personal website saying that Claude, the AI software, had helped prove the Riemann hypothesis. He says that Claude helped develop a solution to the problem during the course of about six weeks.

If Alpöge’s claim is ultimately confirmed, the proof could mark another breakthrough in the use of AI for complicated math problems – even as mathematicians express uneasiness around extremely lucrative private companies dishing out millions of dollars for the technology to solve problems.

Anthropic’s historic stock market debut: key takeaways, and what comes next for the AI industry

Read more

“Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” Alpöge wrote, while anthropomorphizing the AI software. “No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”

Alpöge linked to computer code – written in a language called Lean – that he maintained could verify the findings.

Mathematicians subsequently began working to see if Alpöge’s proof could be confirmed.

Alpöge’s note was published just one day after Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq stock market index. He acknowledged that, writing: “The precise timing is horrible. If I could have, I’d have finished this all much earlier.”

The Riemann hypothesis is a nearly 170-year-old math problem named after Bernhard Riemann, a German mathematician who proposed it in 1859.

The hypothesis deals with prime numbers – whole numbers greater than 1 that can only be divided by themselves and 1. Riemann questioned how often prime numbers appear and how they are distributed along the number line. And he developed a formula for estimating how many prime numbers exist under a specific number.

The Riemann hypothesis is one of the seven Millennium prize math problems selected in 200 by the Clay Mathematics Institute. The institute has offered $1m for each problem solved.

Mathematicians have been attempting to solve this problem for years. The New York Times reported that on Friday, an independent mathematician in Italy released an incomplete proof of the Riemann hypothesis that he said he had been working on for almost 12 years. That mathematician, Alessandro Masullo, said he did not use AI because he did not fully trust the system.

after newsletter promotion

Other mathematicians have expressed discomfort with relying on AI to solve math problems.

In September, Anthropic competitor OpenAI claimed that a non-public version of its AI tools helped solve part of another Millennium prize problem. But it was solved in a way that struck mathematicians and observers in a way many found strange: a near-trillion-dollar private company spent $15m to employ 10,000 AI systems to solve the problem.

Alpöge was working on that separate problem for Anthropic when OpenAI made its announcement.

University of Warwick mathematician James Robinson told the Guardian in September that “it’s frustrating to see these big tech companies burning this fuel up just so that they can show off about how great their latest model is”.

He added: “It seems like immature playground boasting writ large, underpinned by billions of dollars and the potential for significant environmental damage in an age when climate change is probably the biggest challenge we face.”

Man charged with attempted murder after councillor stabbed in Bradford

Arfan Ali, 31, has also been charged with assault and possession of an offensive weapon in a public place

A man has been charged with attempted murder after a local councillor was stabbed while working in the community in Bradford, police have said.

Arfan Ali, 32, is accused of attacking Ibrar Ali, 52, at about 11am on Thursday in the West Yorkshire city.

The alleged attacker has also been charged with assault and possession of an offensive weapon in a public place, West Yorkshire police said.

He appeared at Leeds magistrates court on Saturday, the Crown Prosecution Service confirmed. He was reportedly remanded in custody ahead of his next appearance, at Bradford crown court on 21 December.

A statement on behalf of Ibrar Ali and his family, shared on Friday, said he had been supporting council wardens with community clean-up activities.

They said: “During the incident, Councillor Ibrar intervened to protect a member of council staff and, in doing so, sustained multiple stab wounds.”

The family said the councillor’s injuries were serious but not life-threatening, and that he was in a stable condition in hospital, adding that he was “grateful for the overwhelming kindness shown and hopes to personally thank everyone once he has recovered”.

Officers were called just after 11am on Thursday to reports the councillor had been found seriously injured on Manse Street.

He is believed to have been injured first in Thornbury Avenue before being driven to Manse Street, according to the force.

Emergency services attended and took him to hospital.

items.title: Russia-bound ship attacked in Gulf of Finland
items.summary: Finnish defence forces say that Ukraine was likely behind the drone attack on the vessel.
items.body:
Image source, Finnish Border Guard

Image caption,

The Finnish Border Guard is leading the operations involving the Sparta II

ByHafsa Khalil

Updated 43 minutes ago

A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.

The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.

"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."

Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.

The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.

The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.

This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.

Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."

The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.

It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.

Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.

Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.

Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.

The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.

Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

items.title: Cigarettes on silver platters at Bondi ‘clean’ beauty business lip gloss launch referred for investigation
items.summary: Copini Beauty referred to New South Wales health regulators, while federal government says it is ‘deeply concerned’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast An Australian beauty company that promotes “clean” ingredients “free from skin irritants” has been referred to state health…
items.body:
Photos posted on Copini Beauty’s Instagram account show what appeared to be cigarettes on display with branded Copini match boxes and lipglosses at an event held earlier in November. Photograph: Copini Beauty Instagram

Photos posted on Copini Beauty’s Instagram account show what appeared to be cigarettes on display with branded Copini match boxes and lipglosses at an event held earlier in November. Photograph: Copini Beauty Instagram

Cigarettes on silver platters at Bondi ‘clean’ beauty business lip gloss launch referred for investigation

Copini Beauty referred to New South Wales health regulators, while federal government says it is ‘deeply concerned’

• Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

An Australian beauty company that promotes “clean” ingredients “free from skin irritants” has been referred to state health regulators after appearing to offer cigarettes to guests at a beachside lip gloss launch.

Photos from an event held earlier in November at a venue in Bondi, Sydney show what appears to be loose cigarettes without health warnings on a tiered silver platter alongside a bowl of lip glosses.

It kills two-thirds of lifetime users – so why is smoking cool again?

Read more

“Celebrating the launch of our soft gloss with our community,” one post from the event shared by the Copini Beauty account on Instagram read, with an accompanying carousel of images showing what appeared to be cigarettes on display with Copini-branded match boxes, lipglosses and glasses of wine.

The images are also featured in a highlight reel from the event on the official Instagram page for the brand.

Copini is co-founded by influencer Casey James and product developer Carla McGraw.

Under the Public Health (Tobacco and Other Products) Act 2023, advertising or promoting smoking or the use of tobacco products is prohibited. Both state and federal laws prohibit businesses offering, giving or distributing a free tobacco product.

Any tobacco supplied must also meet strict product standards, such as displaying mandatory graphic health warnings. The cigarettes at the Copini launch do not appear to carry any health warnings on the filter as required, indicating they are illicit products. Buying or supplying illicit tobacco is illegal in Australia, regardless of the quantity.

Cigarettes in Australia cannot legally carry brand logos. The cigarettes appear to carry the Manchester “sapphire blue” branding, one of the most common illicit tobacco products in Australia. They are considered unlabelled under Australian law because they do not carry official government health warnings and compliant packaging.

A spokesperson for the NSW health minister, Ryan Park, said of the event and images: “This has been referred to NSW health’s centre for regulation and enforcement.”

The centre works with state and federal authorities to regulate smoking products and has powers to inspect premises, seize illicit stock, issue fines and prosecute offenders.

A spokesperson for the federal health department said the government is “deeply concerned about advertising or promotion that glamorises smoking or the use of tobacco products, or helps normalise tobacco use, particularly where it might reach young people”.

“There is no appropriate place for tobacco products to be used as a promotional prop or to make smoking appear fashionable or appealing,” the spokesperson said.

“The government strengthened Australia’s tobacco laws to reduce the visibility and normalisation of tobacco products and protect Australians from the harms of smoking.”

skip past newsletter promotion

after newsletter promotion

The spokesperson said allegations of non-compliance with laws are taken seriously, saying the maximum penalty for criminal advertising or sponsorship of tobacco under federal laws is $728,000 for an individual, or $7.2m for a company.

Smoking accelerates ageing and causes more than 16,000 cases of cancer in Australia each year. The display of cigarettes at the launch appears to contradict Copini’s philosophy: “We’re 100% vegan, cruelty-free, and free from skin irritants and endocrine disruptors,” the website says, stating that “clean ingredients” are used in all products.

The company did not respond to requests for comment.

It comes amid growing concerns about the use of cigarettes by brands, and in images of celebrities, especially online, with health experts warning it risks normalising and glamourising smoking.

Becky Freeman, a professor of tobacco control with the University of Sydney, said it was “shocking to see the resurgence” of smoking in pop culture and on red carpets.

“But to see this really local example, in Bondi, shows this is not an international phenomena – it’s happening in a country like Australia where we have low smoking rates through strong regulations and health policies,” she said.

items.summary: GiveSendGo has been accused of facilitating the financing of extremism, but the platform says it does not ‘condone racism, discrimination, hate speech, or violence of any kind’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian neo-Nazis have raised hundreds of thousands of doll…
items.body:
The White Australia party has raised $200,000 for a legal bid to overturn its ban as a hate group. Photograph: d3sign/Getty Images

The White Australia party has raised $200,000 for a legal bid to overturn its ban as a hate group. Photograph: d3sign/Getty Images

Australian neo-Nazis among far-right groups raising hundreds of thousands via global crowdfunding platform

GiveSendGo has been accused of facilitating the financing of extremism, but the platform says it does not ‘condone racism, discrimination, hate speech, or violence of any kind’

• Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australian neo-Nazis have raised hundreds of thousands of dollars on the global crowdfunding platform GiveSendGo, which has been accused of facilitating the financing of hate and extremism.

Of the 68 Australian fundraisers on the site, the White Australia party has raised the fourth-highest amount of money with $200,000 for its high court battle to overturn its ban as a designated hate group.

Neo-Nazi Thomas Sewell’s legal defence fund is sixth at almost $110,000. Sewell pleaded guilty to violent disorder in October. He and others allegedly stormed Camp Sovereignty in 2025 after taking part in an anti-immigration march. Five people were injured.

Go viral for racist behavior, receive $750,000: inside the new extremist crowdfunding campaigns

Read more

GiveSendGo was set up after GoFundMe started cracking down on hate groups. It says its aims are to “share the Hope of Jesus through crowdfunding” and to “stand for freedom”.

Most crowdfunding on the site is for uncontroversial causes – medical procedures, funerals for relatives, saving endangered species or creative projects.

Other asks are overtly political – the top Australian fundraisers are from anti-trans and anti-abortion activists.

Last year a Minnesota woman who admitted calling a child the N-word raised more than US$750,000 on the site to “protect [her] family”.

The co-founder of GiveSendGo, Jacob Wells, defended hosting that fundraiser, saying he believed in “freedom of speech, freedom of association” and that those were foundational tenets of society.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email

In 2022 the US Anti-Defamation League (ADL) Centre on Extremism found GiveSendGo hosted 230 campaigns “operated by or for extremists and their causes”. The centre found crowdfunding platforms had raised more than US$6m for extremist campaigns, and GiveSendGo was responsible for collecting more than 86.5% of that money from 2016 to 2022.

“Extremist campaigns found on these platforms espouse hateful rhetoric including antisemitism, white supremacy, QAnon conspiracies and anti-LGBTQ+ extremism, as well as rhetoric from antisemitic sects of Black Hebrew Israelites,” it found.

In 2023, the Australia/Israel & Jewish Affairs Council (Aijac) called on the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) Australia – which that year featured the Coalition senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price and former prime minister Tony Abbott – to dump GiveSendGo as its gold sponsor because of its use by neo-Nazis and other extremist groups.

A spokesperson for GiveSendGo said it did not “condone racism, discrimination, hate speech, or violence of any kind”.

“We also do not allow fundraisers that promote or glorify violence, raise money for illegal activity, or mislead givers. We follow the laws of the countries we operate in, and we review every reported fundraiser against our terms of service,” the spokesperson said.

“Fundraisers that violate those rules are subject to moderation or removal.”

Dr Matt Wade, a senior lecturer in social inquiry at LaTrobe University, has studied the interaction between crowdfunding platforms and extremist movements.

Speaking broadly about GiveSendGo, not specifically about Australia, he said platform’s policies and how they are enforced had “gravely serious implications” and that GiveSendGo’s claim to be a free speech defender made it a “safe haven for white supremacist and neo-Nazi causes”.

Hosting a fundraising campaign tacitly lent any cause legitimacy, he said.

“Crucially, in key cases that are harbingers of growing far-right influence, these donations are not simply expressions of sympathy or support, but outright endorsements of the actions that the beneficiaries took,” he said.

skip past newsletter promotion

after newsletter promotion

GiveSendGo says in its terms of service that it reviews every fundraiser and verifies the recipient’s identity, and that funds are disbursed to the recipient only once they have completed a compliance process.

It expects donors to give only to those they know and trust, and does not confirm that every statement in a fundraiser is true.

It bans any fundraisers for abortion, gender reassignment for minors and anything illegal.

The spokesperson said people had a right to ask for help, others had the right to decide whether to give, and that GiveSendGo was “not a place of judgment but a place of generosity”.

Wade said GiveSendGo’s claim to ban the promotion of racism was questionable.

“Many would argue that, at best, the qualifier of ‘stated or demonstrable purpose’ is wilfully naive and far too narrowly construed, given the ultimate aspirations and raison d’être of some of the figures they host on their platform,” he said.

The top Australian fundraiser currently on the site is for Sall Grover, founder of the Giggle for Girls app, with almost $2m raised. Grover is fighting the federal court finding that her app discriminated against trans woman Roxanne Tickle.

Next is the anti-abortion activist Joanna Howe, who has raised almost $400,000 to pursue legal action under the Fair Work Act against her employer, Adelaide University, because of its investigations into almost 200 allegations against her.

Her husband, James Howe, has raised another $180,000 for a potential defamation case.

Both Howes say on the site they would use any money left over to “transition” their careers.

The Sedra family has raised about $340,000 for help to “move to a safe home”. Andrew and Noleen Sedra, a married couple who are both pastors at the Pentecostal Echo church in Sydney, claim they were threatened at their home by “LGBTQ left-wing activists”. Other reports have cast doubt on that claim.

The Sedras were contacted for comment.

items.title: Louisiana man charged with killing woman on hiking trail and murdering co-worker with crossbow
items.summary: Jared Schurr arrested in Mississippi after Lizeht Rodriguez and Woodrow Scott died in otherwise unrelated killings A man recently strangled a woman to death whom he did not know along a hiking trail north of New Orleans – then killed his co-worker with a crossbow two days later before being arrested…

Police say Schurr confessed to killing Rodriguez in the Northlake nature center north of New Orleans. Photograph: José Luis Magaña/AP

Police say Schurr confessed to killing Rodriguez in the Northlake nature center north of New Orleans. Photograph: José Luis Magaña/AP

Louisiana man charged with killing woman on hiking trail and murdering co-worker with crossbow

Jared Schurr arrested in Mississippi after Lizeht Rodriguez and Woodrow Scott died in otherwise unrelated killings

A man recently strangled a woman to death whom he did not know along a hiking trail north of New Orleans – then killed his co-worker with a crossbow two days later before being arrested in Mississippi after a police chase, authorities allege.

Jared Schurr, 36, faces counts of second-degree murder in the killings of Lizeht Rodriguez, 24, and Woodrow Scott, 37, on 11 and 13 November, respectively, investigators said on Saturday.

Lizeht Rodriguez. Photograph: gofundme

As described by officials, Rodriguez’s death is a chilling example of a case not often seen in the US: a random murder by a stranger.

Rodriguez body was found slain at the Northlake nature center in Mandeville, Louisiana. On Saturday, detectives with the local St Tammany parish sheriff’s office major crimes unit obtained an arrest warrant accusing Schurr of second-degree murder in connection with Rodriguez’s death, the agency said in a statement.

The statement said: “Schurr confessed to encountering Rodriguez, whom he did not know, while walking along a trail at the Northlake nature center.

“Schurr told detectives he passed Rodriguez on the trail before grabbing and strangling her, then dragging her body to the area where she was later discovered by another person walking along the trail,” the statement continued.

At the time that St Tammany investigators obtained that warrant, Schurr was already wanted by the sheriff’s office in connection with a separate homicide that occurred two days after Rodriguez’s killing.

Jared Schurr. Photograph: St Tammany parish sheriff's office

Schurr in that case is suspected of shooting his co-worker Scott in the back with a crossbow. He was arrested on 13 November after a vehicle chase that began near Bogalusa, Louisiana – north of Mandeville – and ended in Pearl River county, Mississippi.

As of Saturday, Schurr was being held in custody in the Pearl River jail pending extradition to Louisiana.

Authorities said they homed in on Schurr after an investigation involving assistance from the FBI and license-plate reading cameras.

The St Tammany parish sheriff’s office said its detectives were awaiting the results of DNA analysis which were expected to provide additional evidence linking Schurr to Rodriguez’s murder. The agency also said it would continue looking into both homicides to determine what the motive may have been.

FBI research estimates that fewer than 10% of murder victims are killed by people not known to them. The vast majority of people murdered are instead victimized by people they know, according to that research.

Barnham’s symbolic referendum asked residents whether they supported seeking a crown dependency status – a system similar to that of Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man – which would allow the village to ‘retain loyalty to the crown’. Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images

Suffolk village votes to ‘leave the UK’ over plans to house asylum seekers nearby

Local MP says legitimate criticisms of asylum housing plans are being co-opted by opposition parties ‘stirring up racial discord’

Residents of a Suffolk village have voted to “leave the UK” in a referendum held in response to government plans to house 930 asylum seekers at a nearby former military base.

Approximately 500 people in Barnham were eligible to take part in the symbolic vote on Saturday. There were 257 votes for independence, 16 against and one spoiled ballot.

After the vote, Helen Beck, the chair of Barnham Residents’ Association, said Barnham’s flag would be a stone-curlew on a “Suffolk blue background”.

RAF Barnham was one of three Ministry of Defence sites named in June by the government as potential locations for new developments to house asylum seekers.

The flag of Barnham’s mooted new crown dependency, featuring a stone-curlew against a ‘Suffolk blue background’. Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images

A similar referendum was held in Piddington, Oxfordshire in September, with residents also voting to leave the UK amid plans to house more than 1,000 migrants at another former military base.

In Barnham, the plans have prompted protests outside the site. The referendum asked residents whether they supported seeking a “crown dependency status”, which is a similar system to that of Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man.

John Bauer, the parish council chair, said this would allow the village to “retain loyalty to the crown” but remove itself from Home Office jurisdiction.

While in opposition the Labour party had attacked the Conservative policy to house asylum seekers on military bases; once in government, however, the party backtracked. The Conservatives have also reversed their position, with Kemi Badenoch telling frustrated villagers “the Conservative party is on your side”.

“We know that the problem of the boats needs to stop and we have got a plan to stop it,” she said on Friday.

Earlier this month, it was announced construction company Kier would design the new camp at RAF Barnham.

Before Saturday’s vote Labour’s Dr Peter Prinsley, the local MP, said he was against the development of the site. Prinsley said the plans resembled a “concentration camp”, and warned that planning permission may be difficult to attain due to environmental concerns about rare species living in the area – in particular, stone-curlews – with previous development applications nearby having been turned down.

“This is a symbolic referendum,” Prinsley said. “It’s not going to produce a binding result. I’m expecting that [the result] will be hugely in favour of becoming a crown dependency. There are 500 electors, so I’m expecting it to be 500 – nil.”

He added that the government “is doing an awful lot to deal with the irregular migration problem”, and highlighted that net migration may come down to “more or less zero by the end of the year”.

But he added that he didn’t think “the large army camps in remote locations are ever likely to be appropriate for the distribution of people seeking asylum. The fact is that people who arrive here on small boats are not illegal migrants. They are people who are seeking asylum. Our political opponents have described these people as ‘illegals, criminals, rapists’, and all sorts of things that they’re not. They’re just people who have arrived on small boats. The government is getting a grip on this problem, but it’s a complicated problem.”

He said the proposed Barnham site had particular issues which may make it unsuitable. “It’s a remote location without any pedestrian access, it’s on a very hazardous main road. When it was used as military accommodation there were serious accidents on that road.

“It’s also a site of special scientific interest because it is the nesting site for stone-curlews, which will make any planning application very difficult – even a government planning application – because these are worldwide protections.”

He suggested “disused office blocks in some of the larger cities” may be more appropriate places to house asylum seekers, with more local services available.

The permanent protest camp outside the gates of the former RAF base where the Home Office propose to house asylum seekers. Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images

“It feels like a concentration camp,” Prinsley added. “It doesn’t feel like a place that has a compassionate approach to people who are fleeing persecution and are being processed for asylum.”

He also said legitimate criticism of the plans had been co-opted by opposition parties who are aiming to “stir up racial discord”.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “We recognise the strength of feeling in local communities and are listening carefully to the concerns being raised.

“The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1bn saved in costs since the election.

“This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites. These are designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to reduce the impact on local communities.”

items.title: Trump orders contractors to check with White House over any congressional inquiries
items.summary: Anticipating flood of Democratic requests, US president issues executive order in attempt to stymie oversight efforts Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that…
items.body:
Donald Trump at the White House in Washington DC on 5 November. Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters

Donald Trump at the White House in Washington DC on 5 November. Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters

Trump orders contractors to check with White House over any congressional inquiries

Anticipating flood of Democratic requests, US president issues executive order in attempt to stymie oversight efforts

Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to an executive order issued late Friday.

The companies must also coordinate with the White House and US agencies on “appropriate responses” to any such requests, the order says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns, their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.

The order signed late Friday is the administration’s latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets , noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump’s family, particularly at the Pentagon.

It comes as White House officials have already begun taking steps to exert more control over how agencies and officials respond to congressional requests, anticipating there will be a flood of investigations once Democrats take power in January.

On Monday, Will Scharf, the White House counsel, told US agencies that they must seek approval from his office and the White House’s office of legislative affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress. Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to the US representative Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to “blatant criminality”.

Garcia earlier this week sent letters directing members of Trump’s family and top administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, noting in a letter to Democratic lawmakers that they are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance.

In a fact sheet, the White House framed the new requirements as “protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach”, arguing that some congressional leaders have tried to intrude on executive branch privileges by “harassing private companies that contract with the federal government”.

Presidents of both parties have long used executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries, but the claims can set up messy, protracted legal fights as parties dispute whether it applies. Executive privilege allows the president to keep information from the courts, Congress and the public to protect the confidentiality of White House deliberations, but the protection is far from absolute.

Friday’s executive order applies to all contractors and subcontractors, a universe of tens of thousands of businesses.

items.summary: Fausto Isidro Meza Flores was one of FBI’s most wanted fugitives and evaded capture for more than a decade The Mexican military captured one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives during a special forces raid in the Mexican state of Sinaloa on Friday night. Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Cha…
items.body:
Meza Flores and two other alleged gang leaders were arrested after a gun battle in Guasave in Sinaloa. Photograph: FBI

Meza Flores and two other alleged gang leaders were arrested after a gun battle in Guasave in Sinaloa. Photograph: FBI

Alleged Mexican drug cartel boss ‘El Chapo Isidro’ arrested in special forces raid

Fausto Isidro Meza Flores was one of FBI’s most wanted fugitives and evaded capture for more than a decade

The Mexican military captured one of the FBI’s top 10 most wanted fugitives during a special forces raid in the Mexican state of Sinaloa on Friday night.

Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro”, was arrested along with two other alleged leaders of his gang after a gun battle that sparked widespread panic in the city of Guasave.

The alleged leader of a major drug-trafficking cartel, the Meza Flores Transnational Criminal Organization (TCO), he had managed to evade arrest for more than a decade, even though there was a reward of up to $5m (£3.8m) on his head.

Video posted by Mexican authorities shows police leading man away

His FBI “most wanted” poster states his organisation “is allegedly responsible for the possession, distribution, and importation of large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl, and marijuana into the United States, and has predominately controlled drug production, transportation, and distribution in several locations throughout Mexico”.

Mexico’s defence ministry also alleged he is the leader of the Beltrán Leyva criminal organisation, which is allied to the Mayos, one of two rival factions in the powerful Sinaloa cartel.

Meza Flores’s alleged second-in-command, Germán N, whose alias is “Serafín”, and José N, an alleged financial operator for the Beltrán Leyva group, were also arrested.

The operation to capture the men was carried out by “elite military forces” with help from US intelligence, according to Mexico’s defence ministry.

After arriving in the “target area … using stealth and surprise”, the ministry said the arresting force came under attack “with gunfire and explosives” but managed to enter a house and make the arrests.

The men were then evacuated to Mexico City on a Mexican air force plane to be handed over to prosecutors.

Meza Flores’s FBI ‘most wanted’ poster Photograph: FBI

Videos and photos show civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game at Kuroda Park stadium in Guasave, as well as burnt-out cars.

A barrage of rapid fire from what appeared to be Mexican security force helicopters fired at the ground, according to CNN, and players from the Venados de Mazatlán and Algodoneros de Guasave teams abandoned the field mid-game.

Meza Flores was originally indicted in 2012, and in 2013 the US Treasury placed sanctions on him under the Kingpin Act, freezing his assets.

In 2017, the US Department of State’s Narcotics Rewards Program began offering up to $5m as a reward for information leading directly to his arrest or conviction.

He has been charged with multiple counts of drug-trafficking violations and use and possession of a firearm in the US and was wanted in Mexico for organised crime and offences against public health.

items.summary: US vice-president says it’s not his place to second-guess the president, but refrains from endorsing Trump’s claim At a White House news conference on Friday, JD Vance stopped short of endorsing Donald Trump’s claim that Iran was so close to obtaining a nuclear weapon in February that it was essenti…
items.body:
JD Vance, with Marco Rubio and Donald Trump, at a news conference in the White House on Friday. Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/AP

JD Vance, with Marco Rubio and Donald Trump, at a news conference in the White House on Friday. Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/AP

Vance stops short of endorsing Trump’s claim that Iran was close to nuclear weapon

US vice-president says it’s not his place to second-guess the president, but refrains from endorsing Trump’s claim

At a White House news conference on Friday, JD Vance stopped short of endorsing Donald Trump’s claim that Iran was so close to obtaining a nuclear weapon in February that it was essential for the US to go to war with the Islamic republic.

In the White House briefing room, Trump was asked about reporting this week that he was unhappy with the US vice-president’s statement blaming Republican losses in the midterm elections on the Iran war.

“I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” Trump said. “I thought the statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing, that if it were asked, I would have said that: ‘Would you do it again?’ And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

items.title: International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
items.summary: Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’ Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome…
items.body:
UN delegates at the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in Geneva. Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty

UN delegates at the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in Geneva. Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty

International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse

Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’

Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.

Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.

The mandate asked countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.

Although Russia led the objections using obstructive stalling tactics, other military powers invested in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.

Delegates attend the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in Geneva. Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty

Some argued that international humanitarian law was sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a new law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges. European and Nato states, including Ukraine, China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.

The US said the need for human control over autonomous weapons had been discussed at the Apec summit in meetings between president Xi Jinping and Donald Trump this week, but the US was reluctant to agree a binding treaty.

South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany were among the defence tech powers exploring AI-enabled weapons who also expressed resistance to being bound by a new law, instead advocating for a nonbinding agreement.

The CCW is a UN forum that operates via consensus, meaning all 128 parties to the convention have to agree unanimously to pass a statement. The high threshold has resulted in the CCW failing to pass any new laws regulating weapons in the past 30 years and states seeking pathways elsewhere to pass treaties, such as the 2008 ban on cluster munitions.

The Future of Life Institute’s chair, Max Tegmark, said world leaders had failed to meet the moment this week. “Slaughterbots are already here,” he said. “Yet states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about this for the 14th year.”

A campaign billboard is driven past the Houses of Parliament in London calling for control of AI weapons. Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA

Diplomats inside the negotiations said Russia had been deliberately filibustering and not working in good faith, as opposed to the US delegates, who had been seeking a path to reach a consensus statement.

The exclusion of several nonmember countries from negotiations also prompted a rare protest in the chamber on the final day of the conference, with the Egyptian delegation shouting at the conference chair.

Israel and the US have also used AI-enabled targeting systems to conduct tens of thousands of strikes in Gaza and Iran, which have resulted in mass casualties. The Pentagon struck more than 1,000 targets in Iran on the first day of the war, and according to investigative media reports, the US military is aiming to carry out 1,000 AI-assisted targeting decisions per hour.

Critics said this outcome was a missed opportunity, noting that states had been discussing the issue of autonomous weapons, their dangers, and the need for international rules on how to restrict and regulate them for 13 years and large substantive parts of a treaty had already been settled upon.

One European diplomat said: “There was no political will to really regulate these weapons. No will commensurate to the urgency and need.”

A Human Rights Watch’s senior arms adviser, Bonnie Docherty, who had been directly involved in previously successful treaties banning cluster munitions and nuclear weapons, said autonomous weapons needed binding law. She noted that treaties could be negotiated within 15 months and dismissed the US’s proposal of five years to sort out a mandate.

A bloc of seven countries – Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama – had led the push for a binding treaty to be negotiated within one year.

On Wednesday Brazil’s delegate told the floor: “These are not weapons of the future being discussed here, these are already in use and being further developed. We are late in developing these norms and rules to regulate these lethal autonomous weapons systems.”

items.title: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
items.summary: The National Crime Information Center database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

ByJaroslav Lukiv

Updated 1 hour ago

The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media reports, citing two people briefed on the issue.

The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks.

It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US. The agency did not immediately respond to the BBC's request for comment.

When asked about the breach in a Fox News interview on Saturday, President Donald Trump said he had "just heard" about the hack. "I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he said.

"But maybe we'll learn things that we would've never learned otherwise," the president added.

This apparent breach of FBI database comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyberattacks, but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.

White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with US President Donald Trump saying he was not good enough.

In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.

After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.

In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) .

Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.

The USDA has not publicly commented on the issue.

A measles clinic in Andrews, Texas, in 2025. Photograph: Annie Rice/AP

A measles clinic in Andrews, Texas, in 2025. Photograph: Annie Rice/AP

Virginia child dies in state’s first measles-associated death of 2026

Death adds to national measles outbreak that recently cost the US its measles elimination status after 26 years

Virginia reported its first measles-associated death of 2026 ⁠on Friday, involving a child who tested positive for the infectious disease, the state’s health department said.

The department said the child was ⁠age four or younger. It did not disclose additional details, including the child’s vaccination status, citing the family’s privacy.

The death adds to a worsening national measles outbreak that recently cost the US its measles elimination status after 26 years.

US loses measles elimination status amid worst outbreak since 1991

Read more

Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit US state, reported an eighth measles-related death and confirmed 1,631 measles cases as of Friday.

Wisconsin has ⁠also reported two deaths, while New York state recorded its first measles-associated ​death, involving a ​child.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has confirmed six ​measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, though it does not ​specify the states ‌where the deaths were ​recorded.

A discrepancy between ​state and federal death tallies arose after the CDC, under the Trump administration’s health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures.

Virginia has reported 220 measles ⁠cases so far in 2026, including 40 among children four years old or younger and 75 among those age five to 12, state ⁠health department data showed as of Thursday.

Of those cases, 179 involved unvaccinated individuals, 39 were associated with people ‌whose vaccination status was ‌unknown and two occurred with vaccinated individuals.

“Virginia has not had a measles-related death ‌since 1978,” said Frederic Bertley, immunologist and chief executive officer of the Center of Science and Industry. Bertley added that the measles virus infection is both alarming and evidence that measles is gaining a foothold and becoming a growing problem for the US.

Virginia health officials have reported increased measles activity driven largely by outbreaks ‌in the state’s central region. Buckingham county has reported 127 cases, the most in the state, while neighboring Charlotte county has recorded 34 ​cases.

items.title: British man recalls ‘despair’ over son’s death after fall from Cyprus window
items.summary: Joshua Foster tells of moment he ‘lost control’ of two-year-old when he fell from fourth storey of hotel A British father who was fined by the courts after his two-year-old son fell from a fourth-floor window during a family holiday in Cyprus has recalled his “despair” when the boy slipped from his…
items.body:
Joshua Foster arriving at court in Cyprus after pleading guilty to causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act. Photograph: James Manning/PA

Joshua Foster arriving at court in Cyprus after pleading guilty to causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act. Photograph: James Manning/PA

British man recalls ‘despair’ over son’s death after fall from Cyprus window

Joshua Foster tells of moment he ‘lost control’ of two-year-old when he fell from fourth storey of hotel

A British father who was fined by the courts after his two-year-old son fell from a fourth-floor window during a family holiday in Cyprus has recalled his “despair” when the boy slipped from his grasp.

Joshua Foster was handed a €3,000 (£2,500) penalty after he pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act. Prosecutors in Cyprus had refused to drop the case against him.

During recent court proceedings, it was heard that Foster thought the window at the King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas was closed when he approached it with his son, Jaxon, to show him the view of a waterpark.

The 37-year-old “lost control” of him, the Paphos district court was told, before the boy plunged 10 metres (33ft). The fall happened on 12 July, the first day of the Fosters’ family holiday.

The family were on holiday at the King Evelthon Beach hotel in Chlorakas, Cyprus, when the incident happened. Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA

In an interview with the Daily Mail, Foster said: “I have a burden. I’ll have that my whole life. It’s very traumatic. My mind doesn’t want to go there. I just remember the despair of him falling, and watching him fall.

“It was just such a shock … I put him up thinking he was going against a glass pane … and then he wasn’t there.”

The toddler was pronounced dead at Paphos general hospital shortly after he suffered severe cranial injuries when he hit a veranda below.

Foster recalled his outpouring of emotion when he located his son after the fall. “I picked him up. I held him and screamed,” he said. The Essex-born auditor said he and his wife had an hour with their son’s body after he was pronounced dead.

The decision to charge Foster, reported to be a senior accountant at KPMG, was criticised by his legal representatives, as well as human rights defenders, media pundits and diplomats, arguing that it lacked compassion.

The charge Foster accepted is usually levelled in cases involving fatal traffic accidents. It carries a maximum penalty of four years in prison, but the fine he was handed was the lightest sentence possible for the offence.

At his sentencing in October, Judge Froso Christodoulidou ruled that Foster would not be jailed, before describing the incident as a “tragic event”.

The court had heard that, while the presence of alcohol had been detected in Foster’s blood, it was not enough to suggest he was impaired to the point where he had “acted recklessly”.

Foster was detained after the fall. He reportedly had to tell his eldest child, a daughter, about her brother’s death via a video call while he was being held.

He posted €30,000 (£26,000) in bail to return to the UK to attend the funeral of his son in August, but was forced, under threat of extradition, to return to Cyprus and surrender his passport by 14 September.

In a push for clemency, Foster’s legal team had appealed in September to the island’s attorney general, Cyprus’s top legal official, to discontinue the criminal procedure on humanitarian grounds. The request was denied.

Since returning home, Foster said the focus of his grieving family had turned to their daughter.

“It’s very difficult,” he said. “She waves at the sky and says: ‘I love you’ to him and blows a kiss. She’s lost her best friend. She’s gone from having a sibling to being an only child.”

Cold gives way to rain in parts of UK as weather warning issued for south-west England

Flood alerts in place and risk of power cuts as more than 100mm predicted to fall on Dartmoor on Sunday

Cold snaps are to make way for heavy rain in some parts of the country as the Met Office issued a weather warning for south-west England.

It said there will be a slow-moving band of rain moving across Devon and Cornwall, with more than 100mm due to fall on Dartmoor. The warning will be in place from 6am on Sunday until midnight.

The Met Office said there was a risk of power cuts and added that driving conditions could be difficult. There are active flood alerts in the area.

Cold weather health warnings are in place in northern England until Tuesday morning. The lowest temperature this autumn so far was recored on Friday night.

North-west and north-east England, and Yorkshire and the Humber, have had yellow alerts issued by the UK Health Security Agency. It suggests there is a risk to vulnerable people and that conditions may put pressure on the health service and people should take care when travelling.

Friday night had the lowest temperature since early January, as Tulloch Bridge in the Highlands recorded -10.6C. It beat this autumn’s record of -8.4C at the same weather station on Thursday.

A motorist drives through wintry conditions on Snake Pass in Derbyshire 17 November. Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA

The Met Office said there could be a widespread frost across the UK on Saturday night, but there will be warmer and largely drier conditions outside south-west England on Sunday.

The Met Office chief forecaster, Matthew Lehnert, said: “Within the warning area, 20-40mm of rain is likely quite widely, but some parts of south Devon and Cornwall could see 60-80mm.

after newsletter promotion

“Over Dartmoor, there is a chance of more than 100mm falling through the day. This slow-moving band of rain will gradually ease on Sunday night, but flooding and travel disruption is possible within the warning area, with south Devon and south Cornwall more likely to see higher totals.

“There is still some uncertainty about where the heaviest rain will fall, so it’s important to stay up to date with the forecast and any warning updates.”

items.summary: Documentary records Catherine taking on Three Peaks challenge and finding ‘sense of hope alongside uncertainty’ The Princess of Wales has spoken candidly about the impact of her cancer diagnosis in a BBC documentary to be aired later this month. “Cancer does change you,” Catherine, 44, says in the t…
items.body:
The Princess of Wales became the first royal to climb Ben Nevis, Scafell Pike and Yr Wyddfa in less than 24 hours. Photograph: BBC/Kensington Palace/Matt Porteous

The Princess of Wales became the first royal to climb Ben Nevis, Scafell Pike and Yr Wyddfa in less than 24 hours. Photograph: BBC/Kensington Palace/Matt Porteous

Princess of Wales speaks about impact of cancer diagnosis in BBC film Heal

Documentary records Catherine taking on Three Peaks challenge and finding ‘sense of hope alongside uncertainty’

The Princess of Wales has spoken candidly about the impact of her cancer diagnosis in a BBC documentary to be aired later this month.

“Cancer does change you,” Catherine, 44, says in the trailer for the 30-minute programme. “It changes your body. It changes you physically, but there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.”

The film records Catherine taking on the Three Peaks challenge – climbing the three highest mountains in England, Scotland and Wales in 24 hours – and meeting with other people undergoing cancer treatment. Described by the BBC as a “highly personal film”, the documentary, titled Heal, will be shown on BBC One on 29 November.

The Princess of Wales climbing Yr Wydffa in Snowdonia. Photograph: BBC/Kensington Palace/Matt Porteous

The trailer emerged as it was reported that King Charles will voluntarily pay “mansion tax” on relevant royal household properties, despite crown exemption. The high-value council tax surcharge, often referred to as a mansion tax, will take effect in 2028 and apply to properties valued at more than £2m.

Catherine was diagnosed with an undisclosed form of cancer in early 2024, for which she received chemotherapy, and by January 2025 announced she was in remission.

She was treated at the Royal Marsden hospital in London, a world-leading oncology centre, with funds from the distribution of the documentary, which will also be broadcast in other countries, going to the Royal Marsden cancer charity.

When people successfully finish cancer treatment at the hospital they often ring a bell in celebration. “I didn’t ring the bell,” Catherine says in the trailer, speaking to her brother, James Middleton, as they are walking together.

“Maybe this is your ringing the bell,” he says, in reference to her undertaking the Three Peaks challenge and making the programme.

When she completed the challenge in June, 18 months after announcing that the cancer was in remission, she became the first royal to have achieved the feat – climbing Ben Nevis, Scafell Pike and Yr Wyddfa in less than 24 hours, having started on a Saturday evening.

skip past newsletter promotion

after newsletter promotion

Funds from the distribution of the film will go to the Royal Marsden cancer charity where Catherine was treated. Photograph: BBC/Kensington Palace/Matt Porteous

In the programme, which will be introduced by the presenter Kirsty Young, Catherine talks about how she has learned through her recovery to find “a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty”.

Kate Phillips, the BBC’s chief content officer, said she hoped the documentary “will resonate with BBC viewers and provide comfort and support to those navigating their own health challenges”.

items.title: Denmark to expel Russian diplomat over alleged plot to kill US-Ukrainian rapper
items.summary: Moscow intelligence thought to be behind plan to kill musician Kyivstoner before concert in Denmark Denmark’s foreign minister has said Russia’s defence attache in Copenhagen would be expelled after Moscow was suspected of being behind an attempted killing of a US-Ukrainian rapper. “We have just sum…
items.body:
Danish police said they had averted an attempt by Russian intelligence services ⁠to kill Kyivstoner in September. Photograph: Sipa US/Alamy

Danish police said they had averted an attempt by Russian intelligence services ⁠to kill Kyivstoner in September. Photograph: Sipa US/Alamy

Denmark to expel Russian diplomat over alleged plot to kill US-Ukrainian rapper

Moscow intelligence thought to be behind plan to kill musician Kyivstoner before concert in Denmark

Denmark’s foreign minister has said Russia’s defence attache in Copenhagen would be expelled after Moscow was suspected of being behind an attempted killing of a US-Ukrainian rapper.

“We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attache from Denmark,” Lars Løkke Rasmussen told a news conference. The expulsion will happen within seven days.

“We are saying this very clearly: we have exposed you,” he added.

Danish police said they had averted an attempt by Russian intelligence services ⁠to kill the US-Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner in September before a planned performance in Denmark.

Rasmussen also said that Denmark was considering suspending Schengen visas to Russians. “We have launched work at the European level to further tighten the rules governing access of Russian nationals to Europe,” he said. “We are now stepping up our efforts towards a halt to all non-essential visas.

“The strongest response Denmark can give is not to waver and to support Ukraine. And we fully intend to continue supporting Ukraine.”

According to Reuters, Rasmussen sent a message on Friday evening to senior European diplomats ‌proposing that the EU should halt tourist visas for Russian citizens and cease recognition of Russian non-biometric passports throughout the 29-nation Schengen free-travel zone.

Denmark’s foreign minister, Lars Løekke Rasmussen, told Moscow: ‘We are saying this very clearly: we have exposed you.’ Photograph: Emil Nicolai Helms/Reuters

“We must take concrete actions that project European strength ‌and decisiveness,” the message said. “There is clear momentum to act decisively now, and we should seize this moment to replace our current patchwork ​of national measures with a truly unified EU-wide approach.”

The note also urged each EU member state to offer Russians more limited visas that do not allow travel to other countries in the Schengen zone, and to set tougher entry restrictions for serving and former Russian soldiers.

Russian naval aggression prompts new defensive initiative with ‘beer-drinking nations’

Read more

Police ⁠thwarted the alleged ⁠plot when ​they arrested three men with links to the Danish criminal underworld shortly before Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Viktorovich Vasiliev, was due to perform at a ⁠concert on 25 September, which was then cancelled, officials said. Vasiliev holds US and Ukrainian nationality.

Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen, the head of Denmark’s national security and intelligence service, said: “It is our clear assessment that the assassination attempt was planned by the Russian ⁠intelligence services.”

According to prosecutors, the suspects were driving towards the concert venue north of Copenhagen with two loaded pistols and two knives when police arrested them at about 9.55pm, five minutes before the concert was due ‌to begin. A fourth suspect was arrested later that evening, police said.

One of the suspects had bought a ticket to the concert, according ​to the charges.

The suspects are charged under Section 108 of Denmark’s criminal code, which covers assisting a foreign intelligence service, as well as attempted murder. They denied wrongdoing in court, the broadcaster DR reported.

Kieffer-Kristensen said: “A Russian assassination attempt is not something we’ve seen in Denmark before, ⁠and that gives me an impression of an increasingly aggressive and ​risk-taking Russia.

“We believe ​that the case is important ​for understanding the threat that Denmark faces from Russia.”

The European Commission president, Ursula ​von der Leyen, said the EU ​stood in full solidarity with Denmark and with all member states targeted ​by Russian hybrid ‌attacks. She said the ​bloc would soon ​propose a “new European security strategy” to reinforce preparedness and deterrence.

The Russian embassy ⁠in Copenhagen said that Denmark’s accusations were not backed with ​proof.
